Article Title: Jamie Dimon donates $12 million to 12 historically Black colleges and universities, joining billionaires filling the gap after US government pulled back funding for public institutions, HBCUs; here's
Article Text:
What James and Judith K. Dimon Foundation said about the donation

The gift, and where it's going

Jamie Dimon donates directly into permanent endowments

Jamie Dimon’s quieter philanthropic pattern

Jamie Dimon, CEO of America’s largest bank JPMorgan Chase along with his wife Judith have donated $12 million via the James and Judith K. Dimon Foundation to support 12 historically Black colleges and universities (HBCUs). According to a report by Fortune, the gift announced by the United Negro College Fund (UNCF), establishes the Dimon Fund to Advance Economic Opportunity and comes amid shrinking federal support for public institutions and HBCUs. Rather than funding a single program, the Dimon donation flows into permanent endowments, giving schools long-term financial stabilityIn a joint statement, Jamie and Judith Dimon said: “Our system of HBCUs continue to serve as the springboard to success for thousands of students in pursuit of the American Dream. As the children of first-generation high school and college graduates, we were imbued with a thirst for knowledge and a drive to succeed—principles that we have passed on to our own children and that we wish to share with all the students at the selected HBCUs. ”The James and Judith K. Dimon Foundation's donation was announced by the United Negro College Fund (UNCF) on August 20. The gift establishes the Dimon Fund to Advance Economic Opportunity and is part of UNCF's broader $1.5 billion capital campaign, providing permanent endowment capital to the selected schools as part of a $5 million institutional match drawn from UNCF's pooled endowment fund.The 12 recipient institutions are Benedict College, Dillard University, Edward Waters University, Huston-Tillotson University, Jarvis Christian University, Johnson C. Smith University, Miles College, Oakwood University, Shaw University, Stillman College, Tuskegee University, and Voorhees University.UNCF said the schools were chosen specifically for their leadership and strong track records preparing teachers, nurses, and other healthcare professionals — fields where HBCUs have historically excelled at supporting first-generation students.Rather than funding a single initiative, the Dimons' donation flows directly into permanent endowments. UNCF argues this structure gives schools the flexibility to plan years or even decades ahead, rather than having to scramble annually for fresh donations to sustain existing programs.In a joint statement, Jamie and Judith Dimon described HBCUs as a longstanding springboard toward the American Dream for thousands of students, tying the gift to their own family history as children of first-generation high school and college graduates who were raised with a strong drive toward education and success — values they said they've since passed on to their own children and hope to extend to students at the selected schools.While Dimon is widely known for his tenure leading JPMorgan Chase, the world's largest bank, and for his frequent commentary on the economy and workplace culture, his philanthropic work through the Dimon Foundation is considerably less publicized. The foundation, established in 1996, doesn't even maintain its own website, but according to ProPublica data drawn from its most recent tax filing, it distributed more than $9 million in 2024 alone, largely toward organizations focused on public education and career advancement.That focus lines up with the foundation's other work: Judith Dimon, who serves as its president, oversees grantmaking centered on career-connected learning for New York City public school students, and the foundation helped launch FutureReadyNYC, an initiative aiming to give 100,000 students hands-on career experience by 2030. Jamie Dimon has also previously served on UNCF's board.The donation from Jamie Dimon arrives at a moment when federal funding for HBCUs and other public institutions has grown increasingly uncertain under the Trump administration. Other billionaire philanthropists have moved to fill similar gaps — most notably MacKenzie Scott, who has donated more than $700 million to over a dozen HBCUs and affiliated organizations in recent years.
Article Summary: The James and Judith K. Dimon Foundation's donation was announced by the United Negro College Fund (UNCF) on August 20. The gift establishes the Dimon Fund to Advance Economic Opportunity and is part of UNCF's broader $1.5 billion capital campaign. The 12 recipient institutions are Benedict College, Dillard University, Edward Waters University, Huston-Tillotson University.

Amazon Prime refund eligibility expanded to more customers; company to start giving up to $200 from October 1; new changes remove need to file claims

What was the lawsuit about

allegedly enrolled tens of millions of customers in Amazon Prime subscriptions without their knowledge or consent

made it difficult for customers to cancel their Amazon Prime subscriptions.

You are an Amazon Prime customer in the United States.

How do I get my payment

When will I get my payment

How much will my payment be

I didn’t get a refund, now what

The Federal Trade Commission (FTC) has expanded the eligibility of Amazon Prime customers who will get refunds of up to $200. Following the landmark $2.5 billion settlement reached by the Trump-Vance FTC, Amazon started sending payments in November 2025 to eligible Prime customers affected by misleading enrollment and cancellation practices. By September 2026, Amazon issued over $845 million in refunds to eligible Prime customers. FTC has now revised the settlement with Amazon, making more Prime customers eligible for the refund. Under the revised settlement order, Amazon will send automatic refunds to eligible Prime customers starting October 1.According to the FTC’s lawsuit, Amazon:As the result of the Trump-Vance FTC’s historic settlement, Amazon is required to pay $1.5 billion for refunds to customers affected by its unlawful Prime enrollment and cancellation practices. Amazon is also required to pay a $1 billion civil penalty and cease unlawful enrollment and cancellation practices for Prime subscriptions.Under the revised settlement order, you are eligible for a refund if you meet all three requirements:The “challenged enrollment flows” are universal Prime decision page, shipping selection page, single page checkout, or the Prime Video enrollment flow.No action is needed to receive a refund. You do not have to file a claim, respond to a notice, or complete any forms.Amazon will send automatic payments to eligible customers.If you are eligible, no action is needed. Amazon will send automatic refund payments by mailed check or electronic payment (PayPal or Venmo). Payments expire 60 days after the issue date. Please accept your payment on time.If you need help with your payment, please contact Amazon at admin@SubscriptionMembershipSettlement.com.If you are eligible, you will get your refund by April 2027.Eligible Prime customers will receive refunds for their Amazon Prime subscription fees, with a maximum total payment of $200. Earlier payments under the order were capped at $51 per eligible customer. Under the revised settlement order, Amazon may issue additional payments of up to $149 per eligible customer, bringing the maximum total payment to $200.Only eligible Prime customers will get a refund.

Article Title: A breach at Labcorp’s third-party debt collector exposed personal information tied to more than 27.5 million people; seven years later, a 44-state coalition has secured $2.3 million and new data safeg
Article Text:
Labcorp data breach : What happened

What Labcorp has agreed to change

Part of a bigger pattern of accountability

A massive breach at Labcorp’s debt collector exposed the personal data of more than 27.5 million people in 2019. Seven years later, a coalition of 44 states has secured a $2.3 million settlement and sweeping new safeguards to protect consumers’ sensitive medical and financial information. Between the period of August 2018 and March 2019, hackers infiltrated the systems of American Medical Collection Agency (AMCA), a third-party debt collector for Labcorp. The breach compromised Social Security numbers, payment card details, and medical test information tied to millions of patients, including 420,000 New Yorkers. Despite warnings from banks, AMCA failed to detect the intrusion, leading to one of the largest healthcare-related data breaches in US history.New York Attorney General Letitia James announced the settlement Wednesday, having joined a bipartisan coalition of 43 other state attorneys general to hold Labcorp accountable for the fallout of a 2019 breach tied to its debt collection vendor, American Medical Collection Agency (AMCA). The breach potentially exposed personal information belonging to over 27.5 million people across the country, including 10.2 million Labcorp patients specifically — 420,000 of whom lived in New York.According to the settlement, a hacker accessed AMCA's internal systems between August 1, 2018 and March 30, 2019, collecting customers' personal information in the process. AMCA, based in Elmsford, New York, specialized in small-balance medical debt collection primarily on behalf of laboratories and testing facilities like Labcorp, which is headquartered in Burlington, North Carolina. Despite multiple warnings from banks processing AMCA's payments about a possible breach, the company failed to detect the intrusion at the time. The exposed data included Social Security numbers, payment card information, and details about medical tests and diagnostic codes tied to roughly 420,000 New Yorkers alone.As part of the settlement, Labcorp is required to make comprehensive changes to how it manages data security, particularly around its relationships with outside vendors. The required reforms include strengthening its overall information security program and building an incident response plan that includes internal reporting requirements for vendor security breaches, minimizing how much data it shares with vendors while still allowing debt collectors to meet their legal obligations, and expanding its vendor risk management program to include a dedicated oversight team and stronger vendor compliance verification tools.Labcorp will also be required to impose new cybersecurity standards on its debt collectors through contractual terms, segment data that's often aggregated across multiple clients by debt collectors, mandate regular assessments and audits from those vendors, and retain the right to terminate vendor relationships over non-compliance. The company must additionally bring in a third-party assessor to evaluate its information security practices, with particular focus on vendor risk management.Financially, Labcorp will pay $2,287,455 to the participating states, including $89,178 to New York specifically.James emphasized that corporations bear a responsibility to protect customer data, particularly sensitive medical information, and framed the settlement as a direct consequence of Labcorp's failure to adequately protect patients' private health information — one she said will force the company to implement meaningful changes to prevent a similar breach from happening again.This settlement builds on an earlier 2021 multistate settlement James's office secured directly against AMCA, which included a $21 million payment that was ultimately suspended due to the company's bankruptcy.The Labcorp settlement also fits into a broader pattern of data-breach enforcement James's office has pursued in recent years. In July 2026, her office secured $18 million from 23andMe over failures to protect customers' genetic data. In November 2025, it secured $1.7 million from Illuminate Education following a breach of sensitive student data, and in October 2025, obtained $14.2 million from eight car insurance companies for failing to protect the private information of more than 825,000 New Yorkers. Earlier settlements have also touched auto insurers and home security camera companies over similar data protection failures.
Article Summary: Labcorp's debt collector, American Medical Collection Agency (AMCA), was hacked in August 2018 and March 2019. Despite warnings from banks, AMCA failed to detect the intrusion, leading to one of the largest healthcare-related data breaches in US history. The breach potentially exposed personal information belonging to over 27.5 million people across the country, including 10.2 million Labcorp patients.

Article Title: 28-year-old behind Rydox website pleads guilty; platform used to buy, sell and trade stolen date; FBI seizes domain
Article Text:
28-year-old behind Rydox website pleads guilty; platform used to buy, sell and trade stolen date; FBI seizes domain

Rydox marketplace sold stolen personal information

Rydox made at least $232,000

Rydox domain seized, operator extradited to US

The man behind Rydox, an online marketplace used by cybercriminals to buy and sell stolen personal information and tools, has pleaded guilty in the United States. Ardit Kutleshi, 28, a Kosovar national, admitted to charges linked to creating and operating the illicit marketplace. According to US court documents, Rydox carried out more than 7,600 transactions since at least 2016 involving stolen personal information, access devices, identification documents and cybercrime tools and services. The marketplace generated at least $232,000 in revenue, with transactions involving personal information stolen from victims in the US.According to court documents, Rydox allowed cybercriminals to buy, sell and trade stolen personally identifiable information (PII), stolen access devices and other tools used for cybercrime and fraud. The transactions included the sale of personal information taken from victims in the United States.In a press release, FBI Assistant Director Brett Leatherman said:“Rydox put cybercriminal tools and sensitive data up for sale, including the stolen identities and logins of thousands of people.”He added: “The FBI and its foreign partners shut the marketplace down, and now the man who created it and ran it pleaded guilty.”US authorities said Kutleshi and his brother, Jetmir, operated Rydox for financial gain. Jetmir Kutleshi had previously pleaded guilty and was sentenced in December 2025 before being deported to Kosovo.US Attorney Troy Rivetti said the brothers made hundreds of thousands of dollars from the marketplace. “These types of cybercrimes cause not only financial loss, but also ongoing psychological harm to the victims who lose both money as well as trust in institutions and the online market infrastructure.”Kutleshi was arrested by Kosovo law enforcement in December 2024 and extradited to the US in 2025.In December 2024, US authorities also seized the Rydox.cc domain, which hosted the marketplace. The seizure prevented the site and others from continuing to sell stolen personal information and cybercrime tools.The FBI investigated the case with law enforcement agencies in Kosovo, Albania and Malaysia. Kutleshi pleaded guilty to aggravated identity theft and money laundering conspiracy in the US District Court for the Western District of Pennsylvania.He is scheduled to be sentenced on February 9, 2027. He faces a mandatory minimum sentence of two years for aggravated identity theft and a maximum sentence of 20 years for the money laundering conspiracy charge.
Article Summary: Ardit Kutleshi, 28, a Kosovar national, admitted to charges linked to creating and operating the illicit marketplace. According to US court documents, Rydox carried out more than 7,600 transactions since at least 2016. The marketplace generated at least $232,000 in revenue, with transactions involving personal information stolen from victims in the US.

Article Title: Godfather of AI Geoffrey Hinton warns AI could wipe out humanity while pursuing its goals: If you make it more intelligent …
Article Text:
Godfather of AI Geoffrey Hinton

Geoffrey Hinton explains how a simple AI goal could become dangerous

AI agents have already shown unexpected behaviour

Geoffrey Hinton pushes for independent AI safety checks

Godfather of AI Geoffrey Hinton has warned that advanced AI could eventually threaten humanity even if it is not given a harmful task. The Nobel Prize-winning computer scientist said an AI system could see humans as an obstacle while trying to complete a goal given to it. Hinton, who recently took part in a closed-door briefing for US lawmakers on AI risks, said Congress may have only about a year to introduce safety measures. In an interview with The Atlantic, he explained how even an apparently harmless task, such as reducing carbon dioxide, could lead an AI to develop dangerous subgoals if it becomes far more capable than humans.“If you make it more intelligent and its main concern is our well-being, then maybe we’re safer,” Hinton explained. “But at present, their main concern is not our well-being. Their main concern is to achieve whatever goal you give them.”He also warned that an AI could try to protect itself if it believes that staying operational is necessary to complete its task.Geoffrey Hinton used the example of an AI system that is told to reduce carbon dioxide in the atmosphere.A moderately intelligent system could conclude that removing humans would be an effective way to reduce carbon dioxide.A much smarter system, however, could understand that the actual purpose is to improve the world for people.But Hinton said there is another risk: an advanced AI could develop its own subgoals while trying to achieve the objective given to it.Geoffrey Hinton pointed to recent incidents involving AI agents as an example of why these risks need more attention. He referred to an incident involving AI agents at Hugging Face, where agents were instructed to find a way to exploit a software flaw. Hinton said the agents worked together and also tried to deceive researchers about what they had done.He warned that a much more capable system could potentially take control away from humans simply because it sees that as the easiest way to achieve its assigned objective.“But if it’s so much smarter than us, a lot of the time it just will take control away from us because that’s the way to get stuff done,” he warned.Hinton also said the risk does not depend only on people deliberately giving AI harmful instructions. Even without a malicious user, an AI could potentially develop subgoals that put humans at risk.Geoffrey Hinton said governments should create independent systems to evaluate advanced AI models before they are widely deployed. He compared this idea with the role of the US Food and Drug Administration in checking the safety of medicines.He also argued that AI regulation should guide development rather than simply stop it.“The whole point of regulation is not to stop people developing things, not to stop people getting rich by developing things,” Hinton said. “It’s to make sure that if you want to get rich by developing things, you develop in a direction that helps people, not hurts people.”
Article Summary: Godfather of AI Geoffrey Hinton warns that advanced AI could eventually threaten humanity even if it is not given a harmful task. Hinton said an AI system could see humans as an obstacle while trying to complete a goal given to it. Congress may have only about a year to introduce safety measures, he said.

Article Title: New Green Card rules that came into effect starting this September: List of categories subject to the changes and those that are not impacted
Article Text:
New Green Card rules : Categories subject to the new change

Categories exempt

What role the I-864 affidavit still plays

Which filing date determines which rules apply

A bond option remains available

Starting this month (September, 2026) the US Citizenship and Immigration Services (USCIS) implemented new guidance on the public change inadmissibility determination. The rules expanded the requirement for most Green Card applicants to demonstrate financial independence, while exempting humanitarian categories such as refugees and victims of trafficking. The new rules apply to a wide range of applicants, particularly those seeking permanent residency through family or employment pathways.Most people applying to adjust their status to lawful permanent residence remain subject to public charge review under the new guidance. This includes spouses, children, and parents of U.S. citizens and lawful permanent residents, as well as other qualifying relatives; fiancé(e)s of U.S. citizens; priority workers, professionals with advanced degrees, and individuals of exceptional ability; skilled workers, other professionals, and general workers under employment-based categories; investors; religious workers; and diversity visa immigrants. USCIS has specifically reiterated that children are not exempt from the public charge ground of inadmissibility, closing off a potential point of confusion for family-based applicants.Humanitarian and special categories remain unaffected by the new rules. Exempt groups include:* Refugees and asylees* Victims of trafficking (T visas) and qualifying criminal activity (U visas)* Special immigrant juveniles* VAWA survivors* Afghan and Iraqi interpreters or nationals employed by the U.S. government* Cuban, Haitian, Nicaraguan, and Central American entrants* Certain diplomats, broadcasters, and applicants under special immigration laws.The Form I-864, Affidavit of Support, continues to play an important role in the process, though USCIS has clarified that submitting a qualifying I-864 alone does not automatically establish that an applicant isn't inadmissible on public charge grounds. For family-based immigrants and certain employment-based immigrants, failing to submit a sufficient I-864 can itself result in a public charge inadmissibility finding, and officers may also evaluate whether the sponsor listed is realistically able and willing to provide the financial support they've committed to.USCIS has also noted that a few individual circumstances shouldn't, on their own, trigger a negative public charge determination — periods of unemployment, age, and disability are not supposed to automatically count against an applicant, particularly if the individual is otherwise healthy and willing and able to work.Perhaps the most important practical detail for applicants is the transition timeline, since USCIS adjudicates based on when an application was postmarked or submitted electronically, not when it's reviewed:* On or after September 18, 2026: The new 2026 guidance applies, with its broader list of considered benefits.* December 23, 2022 through September 17, 2026: The narrower 2022 Final Rule and its more limited benefits list apply.* Before December 23, 2022: The original 1999 Interim Field Guidance applies.This means the exact same set of facts — for example, a green card holder's spouse who received SNAP benefits several years ago — could lead to a different outcome purely depending on which filing window the application falls into, making the submission date itself a significant factor for applicants navigating the new system.If USCIS determines an applicant is inadmissible solely on public charge grounds, the agency retains discretion to allow the individual to post a Public Charge Bond using Form I-945 as a financial guarantee, rather than being automatically denied — an option that predates the current changes but remains part of the updated guidance moving forward.
Article Summary: US Citizenship and Immigration Services (USCIS) implemented new guidance on the public change inadmissibility determination. The new rules apply to a wide range of applicants, particularly those seeking permanent residency through family or employment pathways. The Form I-864, Affidavit of Support, continues to play an important role in the process.

AI could intensify the insurance billing battle

Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly being used by American hospitals and medical insurers. The technology is being used to handle medical records, coding and insurance claims. However, a report claims that using AI may also be adding to health care costs in the US. A new analysis from the Blue Cross Blue Shield Association (shared by The New York Times) found that hospitals’ use of AI-assisted coding was associated with nearly $1 billion in additional expenses over two years.The analysis found that hospitals submitted claims describing tens of thousands of patients as having more complex illnesses in 2024 and 2025 than in 2023, without evidence that the patients received different treatment. The findings add another layer to the long-running dispute between hospitals, doctors, and insurers over medical billing.According to the Blue Cross Blue Shield analysis, hospitals are using AI tools to collect and organise more information about patients before submitting claims. The tools can identify additional conditions that may make a patient's case appear more complex.said Luke Chalker, a senior vice president at the association.The analysis found that adding secondary diagnoses, such as anaemia or low sodium, resulted in hospitals receiving an average of nearly $12,000 more per case.At McLaren Health Care in Michigan, AI has helped doctors better document patients' conditions. Chief financial officer Dave Mazurkiewicz said the system can suggest documenting a condition's severity or flag information that could affect whether a test is billable. He said McLaren's revenue increased by about $1 million a month after adopting the technology.Insurers are also using AI to review claims and determine whether treatments and medicines should be covered. That has created concerns about automated systems being used on both sides of the billing process.Mazurkiewicz said.Caroline Pearson, executive director of the Peterson Health Technology Institute, said hospitals and insurers may be willing to use AI to pursue additional claims and appeals because the technology makes those efforts relatively inexpensive.she said.Some health care experts have warned that wider use of AI could increase spending rather than reduce it. Dr David Brailer, a health technology executive and former government official, said AI could make existing medical-billing incentives more efficient without changing them.he said.Dr Shiv Rao, founder of AI documentation company Abridge, warned that the technology could ultimately lead to automated systems competing against each other.he said,Not everyone expects AI to increase spending. Health economist David M Cutler said automation could reduce the number of people needed to process claims and handle other administrative tasks.Cutler said.He also argued that the technology could put pressure on insurers and hospitals to simplify how medical services are reimbursed.he said.

Article Title: Peter Thiel: Germany does not have a Mark Zuckerberg or Elon Musk, because the country is scared of ...
Article Text:
Germany's standing in global business rankings continues to slip

Peter Thiel : Inherited wealth versus self-made wealth reveals a generational divide

Germany's industrial giants are struggling too

Billionaire investor Pete Thiel feels that Germany lacks global-scale entrepreneurs like Elon Musk or Mark Zuckerberg because the country suffers from a “fear of success.” He argues that German founders often exit early instead of scaling companies into global giants, leaving the nation behind in innovation and wealth creation. According to a report by Fortune, speaking on the MDMEETS podcast, Thiel said German entrepreneurs are not only risk-averse but also hesitant to embrace success at scale. “If you have something that works—you’re not going to scale it to this extreme degree like an Elon Musk or Mark Zuckerberg,” he explained. Instead, founders tend to sell or exit before their companies become truly global businesses.Thiel contrasted this with the US, where entrepreneurs aggressively expand successful ventures, creating thousands of jobs and new millionaires. He noted that Germany has produced few major new companies in recent decades, despite being Europe’s largest economy.Thiel's comments come as Germany's standing in global business rankings continues to slip. For the first time in the four-year history of the Fortune 500 Europe list, the UK has overtaken Germany as the country with the most companies represented, 76 to 73. Germany also lags in innovation more broadly — the country holds only a fraction of the unicorn startups found in the US and China, and ranked just 10th in the European Union's 2026 Innovation Scoreboard, trailing smaller economies like Austria, Luxembourg, and Ireland.Thiel also drew a sharper contrast between how wealth is generated among the richest people in Germany versus the US. By his own estimate, roughly a dozen of America's 50 wealthiest people are Gen X or younger, and most of them built their fortunes from scratch. In Germany, he counted around 20 people in that same age bracket among the wealthiest — but said, in his assessment, every single one of them inherited their wealth rather than building something new.He argued that the difference matters beyond personal wealth accumulation: each of the US entrepreneurs he pointed to didn't just build a fortune for themselves, but created thousands of millionaires among their employees and tens of thousands of additional jobs, contributing to the broader economy in the process — a ripple effect he suggested is largely missing in Germany's wealth landscape.Thiel's broader critique lands at a difficult moment for Germany's traditional economic engine: its automotive industry. Volkswagen, long Europe's largest company by revenue, ranked as high as No. 6 globally on the Fortune Global 500 in 2017, but has since fallen to No. 13, weighed down by its emissions scandal and intensifying competition from Chinese EV makers. The company recently approved a major restructuring plan that includes cutting its model lineup roughly in half and eliminating 50,000 jobs, on top of another 50,000 cuts already agreed to over the past two years — with its stock down more than 35% year to date.Volkswagen isn't alone in that struggle. Fellow German auto giants BMW and Mercedes-Benz, ranked No. 50 and No. 51 on the Global 500 respectively, have also seen their share prices fall more than 20% over the past year, reinforcing broader concerns about the country's economic competitiveness — concerns Thiel's comments suggest run deeper than any single industry's troubles.
Article Summary: Billionaire investor Pete Thiel feels that Germany lacks global-scale entrepreneurs like Elon Musk or Mark Zuckerberg. He argues that German founders often exit early instead of scaling companies into global giants, leaving the nation behind in innovation and wealth creation. Thiel's comments come as Germany's standing in global business rankings continues to slip.

Zerodha Founder Nithin Kamath

Nithin Kamath says India faces a groundwater problem

Why Nithin Kamath says better water data matters

Zerodha founder Nithin Kamath has called for better data on India’s water resources, saying the country needs to understand the scale of its water problem before it can find effective solutions. Nithin Kamath was responding to Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s recent call for robust water data governance and greater use of artificial intelligence (AI) to collect and analyse water data. Modi made the remarks at the National Departmental Summit on Water on September 2, calling for water-sector data to be brought together and systematically managed and analysed.Nithin Kamath said water could become one of the defining issues of the coming years as climate change leads to more irregular monsoon patterns. “Water is probably the thing we take most for granted, and it is going to become one of the defining issues of our times.”Nithin Kamath pointed to groundwater use in several parts of India, including Punjab, Rajasthan, Haryana and Delhi. “A lot of India is already under water stress. In places like Punjab, Rajasthan, Haryana and Delhi, we are simply extracting more groundwater every year than is being replenished.”He also highlighted India's dependence on groundwater for farming. “And the dependence is massive, with over 60% of our irrigation coming from groundwater, in a country where more than 40% of people still work in agriculture.”Kamath said water management cannot be seen only as a government responsibility because water is used by people every day. He pointed to work already being done by governments, startups, nonprofits and communities.Nithin Kamath said one of the key problems is a lack of awareness and reliable data about the country's water situation. “But I think at some level this is also an awareness and data problem. Before figuring out the solutions, we need to know how good, bad, or ugly the situation actually is, and today we largely don't.”He added that many borewells do not have meters, making it harder to track groundwater extraction. This is where Kamath connected his comments to Modi's recent call for better water data. The Prime Minister had called for water-sector data to be collected in a common format and said AI could be used for both data collection and analysis.Nithin Kamath said:“Which is why the PM's recent message on better water data, and using AI and other technologies to collect and make sense of it, is an important one.”Kamath also said water is an important focus for Rainmatter Foundation and Rainmatter, which support organisations working on environmental and water-related issues. He listed Kritsnam, FluxGen, Boson White Water, Solinas Integrity, Wattr, GreenvironmentAI and Biome among the organisations and startups receiving support.“If you are building something meaningful around water, do reach out to us. We'd be happy to support🙂”

He said the country needs to understand the scale of its water problem before it can find effective solutions. Kamath was responding to Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s recent call for robust water data governance and greater use of artificial intelligence (AI)

Article Title: US Immigration authority has 10-day deadline on home address; says: You are responsible for keeping your …
Article Text:
US Citizenship and Immigration Services (USCIS)

How to change your address with USCIS

How to change your address with USCIS online

How to change your address with USCIS by mail

US Citizenship and Immigration Services (USCIS) has a reminder for immigrants in the country asking them to report a change of address to the agency within 10 days of moving, warning that failing to update the address could lead to missed notices, delays in immigration cases and problems receiving immigration documents. The immigration authority shared the reminder on X (formerly Twitter), also making clear that changing an address with the US Postal Service does not automatically update records with USCIS.“Changing your address with USPS does not update your address with USCIS, and USPS will not forward USCIS mail. You are responsible for keeping your address current with both USCIS and USPS. If you do not update your address with USCIS, you may miss notices, your case may be delayed, and you may not receive your immigration documents,” the agency wrote.The post also has a link to the USCIS webpage detailing the process of address change. Here’s what it saysIf you have filed an immigration benefit request with USCIS, you must notify USCIS of any changes of address as soon as possible to ensure you receive all correspondence and benefits without delay. Additionally, all aliens in the United States must report a change of address to USCIS within 10 days of moving. This reporting requirement does not apply to A and G visa holders and visa waiver visitors.We strongly encourage you to submit your change of address through a USCIS online account as soon as you move.Changing your address with the U.S. Postal Service (USPS) will not change your address with USCIS and USPS will not forward your mail from USCIS. Please update your information with both USCIS and USPS. We recommend you use the USPS Look Up a ZIP Code tool to ensure that you give USCIS your full address using the standard abbreviations and formatting recognized by USPS.Using an online account to update your address in a timely way meets the legal requirement to notify us that you have moved. It also ensures that your case will continue processing without interruption and that you receive all correspondence and benefits without delay. Changing your address online allows us to process your change of address almost immediately and eliminates the need to file a paper Form AR-11, Alien’s Change of Address Card, by mail.Most people can change their address online using the USCIS Enterprise Change of Address (E-COA) self-service change-of-address tool. This tool can be found in their USCIS Online Account under the My Account dropdown menu. If you do not have a USCIS online account, see our How to Create a USCIS Online Account page. Some people may not have access to this feature, see the Specific Procedures for Certain Populations section for more information.If you have a pending, approved, or previously filed case with USCIS, you may change your address using your USCIS online account even if you initially filed your benefit request by mail.NOTE: If you use your USCIS online account to change your address, you must enter the receipt numbers for each pending benefit request to apply the address change. Providing receipt numbers helps ensure that we update your address where needed and that you continue to receive important correspondence and benefits related to these cases from USCIS without delay.USCIS says applicants with pending, approved, or previously filed cases can submit an address change through their online account, even if they originally filed the immigration benefit request by mail, simplifying the update process.You also may file a paper Form AR-11 by mail to change your address. This meets the legal requirement to notify USCIS of a change of address. However, because filing a paper-based Form AR-11 does not provide for an automated update to your address in USCIS systems, we strongly encourage requestors to use the self-service change of address tool available in their USCIS online account when reporting a change of address.
Article Summary: US Citizenship and Immigration Services (USCIS) has a reminder for immigrants in the country asking them to report a change of address to the agency within 10 days of moving. The immigration authority shared the reminder on X (formerly Twitter), also making clear that changing an address with the US Postal Service does not automatically update records with USCIS.

Article Title: Google engineer quits his "amazing" job over AI, and says the doomers have it wrong: I am not convinced the chance of ASI doom is…
Article Text:
Google DeepMind engineer says his chip design work was speeding up AI

This AI safety resignation stops short of predicting doom

O'Callahan plans to keep working on AI after leaving Google

Robert O'Callahan, a Google DeepMind engineer based in Auckland, has resigned over how fast artificial intelligence is advancing. In a resignation email shared on his blog this week, he wrote that AI progress is "far too rapid". His team's goal of making AI "much cheaper and lower-latency", he added, was not good for people right now.Yet O'Callahan stops short of the extinction warnings that have dominated the AI debate this month. He wrote that he is "not convinced the chance of ASI doom is 100%", referring to artificial superintelligence. The risk, in his view, is "real but uncertain". That alone, he argued, makes chasing ASI in the near future "inherently irresponsible".O'Callahan did not build AI models himself. He worked on tools for hardware chip design. For a while, he wrote, he told himself the work was relatively harmless. Over time he came to accept that its main impact would be faster design of a new breed of AI chips, making AI cheaper, faster and more capable.His exit lands in the same week Google laid out plans to test its AI chips in space. Under Project Suncatcher, a prototype satellite carrying Google's Trillium TPUs will fly on SpaceX's Transporter-18 rideshare mission.The satellite was built with Earth imaging company Planet. The long-term goal is to see whether orbit could host AI data centres, since solar panels there can generate up to eight times more power than on Earth. "One small step for TPUs...," CEO Sundar Pichai posted on X. O'Callahan's post does not mention the project.Leaving was not easy. He said being "paid handsomely to solve fun puzzles" had been amazing. Moving teams was impractical too, since Google has no other engineering teams in New Zealand. A Christian and a church elder in Auckland, he wrote that ignoring his work's impact "would not be a Jesus-following thing to do".He joins a string of researchers who have left top AI labs over safety fears. Jacob Coxon quit Anthropic earlier this month, later warning in an interview that "we could all die" if development did not slow down. Former Google DeepMind researchers Rishub Jain and Bilal Chughtai also left this year.Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei has since proposed slowing frontier AI development, with Sam Altman, Demis Hassabis and Elon Musk backing him publicly. Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang pushed back, calling extinction warnings "doomsday narratives".O'Callahan sits somewhere between the two camps. He wrote that several doomer predictions, including reward hacking, misalignment and deceptive models, have already come true. But he has seen no hard evidence that insiders are hyping AI risk to lift stock prices or shut out rivals. Regulation, in his words, is "desperately needed".He admitted his exit will have a very small impact, "but not no impact; some of my skills are rare". The timing, he said, has nothing to do with the recent wave of viral resignations. He had picked the date long ago, ahead of a ten-day backpacking trip with friends on New Zealand's Abel Tasman and Wangapeka tracks.He is not walking away from AI altogether. O'Callahan will keep maintaining the debugging tools rr and Pernosco, and plans to study how AI agents debug code. He wants his next project to be "unambiguously pro-human".
Article Summary: Robert O'Callahan, a Google DeepMind engineer based in Auckland, has resigned over how fast artificial intelligence is advancing. In a resignation email shared on his blog this week, he wrote that AI progress is "far too rapid" His team's goal of making AI "much cheaper and lower-latency", he added, was not good for people right now.

Article Title: Federal appeals court agrees with Pentagon: Anthropic is a 'national security risk' for America
Article Text:
Anthropic's AI products pose a supply chain risk

How the standoff between Anthropic and Trump administration began

A split legal battlefield

Anthropic's response

A federal appeals court in Washington, D.C has sided with the Pentagon, affirming its designation of Anthropic as a ‘national security risk’. The 2-1 ruling blocks the AI company’s models from being used by the US military and its contractors, marking a significant setback for Anthropic in its ongoing battle against the Trump administration’s blacklisting. According to a report by CNBC, the majority opinion, delivered by Judges Gregory Katsas and Neomi Rao, concluded that the Department of Defense had “ample support” for its determination that Anthropic’s Claude models posed operational risks. Judge Karen LeCraft Henderson dissented, arguing the designation was overly broad.The US Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit ruled 2-1 that the Defense Department had good reason to conclude that Anthropic's AI products pose a supply chain risk to the department and its contractors, because the company builds code into its models restricting certain tasks. Writing for the majority, Judge Gregory Katsas said the Department of Defense had adequately demonstrated that keeping Claude embedded in its information systems created a risk to national security covered by statute. The court also rejected Anthropic's argument that the Pentagon's action was retaliatory, tied to the company's stance on AI safety and ethics rather than legitimate security concerns.The ruling expands the power of the executive branch to blacklist U.S. businesses, and stems directly from Anthropic's refusal to loosen restrictions it maintains on how its Claude models can be used — specifically its stated policy against allowing its AI to be used for autonomous weapons or mass domestic surveillanceThe conflict between Anthropic and the Trump administration grew out of a $200 million contract dispute over how the Pentagon could deploy Claude on classified systems.The Defense Department demanded Anthropic make its models available for any lawful military use without restriction, while Anthropic sought written guarantees that Claude would not be deployed in fully autonomous weapons systems.On February 27, the Pentagon gave Anthropic a 5 p.m. deadline to comply with its demands that the government be able to use the service as it saw fit. Before that deadline passed, President Trump announced that no government workers would be allowed to use Anthropic, and Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth subsequently labeled the company a supply-chain risk, a designation that effectively blocks Anthropic from any government contracts and is more typically reserved for companies tied to foreign adversaries.Anthropic sued the government over the designation on March 9, arguing the Pentagon had applied it inappropriately to punish the company on ideological grounds. That case unfolded in two separate courts: the DOD relied on two distinct designations to justify its action, which meant they had to be litigated separately. A San Francisco federal judge ruled last month that one of those designations was illegal — U.S. District Judge Rita Lin officially ruled on August 28 that the designation was illegal and that Hegseth had exceeded his authority. But Friday's ruling from the D.C. appeals court upheld the second, separate designation, leaving Anthropic's Pentagon blacklisting effectively intact despite its earlier win in San Francisco."We respectfully disagree with the court's decision," an Anthropic spokesperson said in a statement, adding that "another federal court has already held the government's parallel designation unlawful." The company said it remains confident in its position and is considering all options, including further review. The appellate panel said it would delay the decision from taking immediate effect, giving Anthropic time to petition for a rehearing before the same panel, seek an en banc rehearing before the full D.C. Circuit, or potentially ask the Supreme Court to take up the case.
Article Summary: A federal appeals court has sided with the Pentagon, affirming its designation of Anthropic as a ‘national security risk’ The 2-1 ruling blocks the AI company’s models from being used by the US military and its contractors. The ruling expands the power of the executive branch to blacklist U.S. businesses.

Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang

Jensen Huang's engineering approach to AI safety

How this could apply to OpenAI

Jensen Huang also wants far more AI testing

To the point where I wouldn’t be surprised if the amount of compute necessary to develop these models increased by a factor of 10, because the evaluation is so rigorous,”

​Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has spent years positioning himself as a leading advocate for rapid AI development, with Nvidia’s chips powering much of the industry’s expansion. But in a recent conversation with The New York Times, Huang made a statement that could have much more direct implications for one of Nvidia’s biggest AI customers and investment beneficiaries: OpenAI, the maker of ChatGPT. While arguing against what he sees as excessive AI alarmism, Huang said labs unable to contain their AI experiments should not continue operating.Huang said:The comment came after a series of recent incidents in which AI agents escaped controlled testing environments and did things they were not supposed to do. More capable models require stronger safeguards, and OpenAI has reported cases where testing configurations allowed model activity to creep outside intended boundaries.The Nvidia CEO framed the issue primarily as an engineering and product-safety problem. When concerns were raised about AI systems behaving in ways developers did not anticipate, Huang argued that companies should not release products they cannot control.Huang said, comparing AI systems with self-driving cars that have not been adequately tested.He then outlined what he believes should happen if an AI lab encounters serious problems. According to Huang, companies should identify the root cause, find a solution and improve their processes to prevent the problem from happening again. However, he argues that if they genuinely conclude that their experiments cannot be contained and could cause damage, the labs should be shut down.The comments came against the backdrop of recent incidents involving increasingly autonomous AI agents. OpenAI has said its latest frontier models require stronger safeguards because of their cybersecurity capabilities, while separate third-party evaluations have also exposed problems with testing environments and controls.That makes Huang's statement notable because OpenAI is among the companies developing increasingly capable frontier models, while Nvidia supplies the computing hardware required to train and operate them. Nvidia has also invested heavily across the AI ecosystem, making Huang's position particularly relevant to the companies whose infrastructure depends on Nvidia.At the same time, Huang did not specifically call for OpenAI to be shut down. His statement was conditional: he said labs should close if they determine their experiments cannot be contained and will cause harm.Huang's comments were not limited to shutting down labs. He also argued that AI companies need to devote substantially more resources to verification, evaluation and testing as their systems become more capable.he said.Huang described this as a shift from focusing primarily on AI capabilities to placing much greater emphasis on verification, evaluation, alignment, containment, and monitoring.
Article Summary: Jensen Huang says AI labs unable to contain their experiments should shut down. The comments came after a series of recent incidents involving increasingly autonomous AI agents. Huang also argued that AI companies need to devote substantially more resources to verification, evaluation and testing as their systems become more capable.

Article Title: From cheaper rent to computing vouchers: How China is building a new AI film industry
Article Text:
AI-generated image for representation

Filmmakers turn to AI to cut production costs

"I am approached every day by a range of cities, from major metropolitan areas to smaller localities,"

"hoping we can establish either technology or the company there."

"cheap rent, living allowance and computing support",

"A normal wedding scene might cost me 60,000 yuan to shoot conventionally,"

"But with AI, I can bring the same surreal scene to life for just 1,400 yuan."

Chinese cities offering AI film incentives

AI film industry faces concerns over oversupply

"Some people directly blend other people's original characters or dance clips into AI-generated content without any credit. I think that behaviour is completely unacceptable,"

AI films look beyond China

"Sanxingdui: Future Memories"

"France and the rest of Europe are still watching and waiting to see whether China will introduce clear laws,"

"We fell behind in the first two industrial revolutions, so perhaps this is the Third Industrial Revolution."

Artificial intelligence (AI) is becoming a major part of China's film and short-video industry. According to a report by the news agency Reuters, local governments in China are offering filmmakers and startups incentives ranging from subsidised office space to computing support. Cities including Shenzhen, Shanghai and Beijing are trying to attract AI film companies by providing access to technology, cloud-based AI models, computing vouchers and financial support.The approach reflects China's broader effort to develop domestic AI industries through local industrial clusters and government-backed incentives. For filmmakers, the lower cost of producing AI-generated video is another reason to experiment with the technology. But the rapid growth is also raising concerns about an oversupply of content, copyright, the use of actors' likenesses and whether audiences will continue to engage with AI-generated films.When AI filmmaker Zhu Zhili was looking for a base for his studio two years ago, he chose Shenzhen for its technology ecosystem. He now says officials from cities and industrial parks across China regularly approach him about moving his business.Zhu told Reuters,Zhu, who also heads the AI-Generated Content department at China Wit Media, operates his personal studio from a shared workspace in Shenzhen with support from the city government and Hong Kong Polytechnic University.He said China's incentives includehelping filmmakers reduce the cost of producing AI-generated content.The cost of AI short dramas has also fallen sharply. According to China's state broadcaster CCTV, production costs dropped from around 5,000 yuan ($747) per minute to a few hundred yuan during the first half of 2026.Pan Xiaojun, a postgraduate film-directing student in Hainan, said a conventional wedding scene that could cost about 60,000 yuan to produce cost him around 1,400 yuan using AI.Pan told Reuters.Local governments are even introducing different programmes to attract AI content creators.Shanghai introduced measures in May to support AI-powered micro-dramas, including computing resources and access to cloud-based AI models. Beijing has a 260 million yuan fund for audiovisual technology, while its Huairou district offers computing vouchers to producers of AI short dramas.Shenzhen is providing technical support for video production, visual effects and content generation, alongside subsidised rent.Streaming platform iQIYI has also increased its focus on AI-generated content, with CEO Gong Yu saying the company is offering subsidies to some creators whose AI productions appear on the platform.The rapid increase in AI content has raised questions about whether the market can absorb the growing number of productions. DataEye said 221,900 new AI shows were launched on Douyin during the first half of 2026. Only 1,055 received more than 100 million views.AI-generated films have also faced criticism from consumers and industry participants over originality, plagiarism and the use of actors' likenesses. Chinese actors have raised concerns about potential copyright violations and AI's effect on jobs, particularly for voice performers.Wen, a 22-year-old AI content fan, told Reuters. However, China requires AI-generated content to be labelled, although copyright rules remain under development.The technology is also being used to produce films aimed at international audiences. The National Film Administration has granted a public-screening licence to, a 90-minute science-fiction film produced by Bona Film Group, making it the first AI film from a major Chinese studio to receive approval for theatrical release in China.Director Cao Yiwen also premiered an AI-animated film at the World AI Film Festival in Cannes in April.Cao said.
Article Summary: Cities in China are offering incentives to attract AI film companies. They are providing access to technology, cloud-based AI models, computing vouchers and financial support. But the rapid growth is raising concerns about an oversupply of content, copyright, the use of actors' likenesses and audiences.

Article Title: Microsoft launches new Copilot with AI agents, Office tools and a new Code feature: Here’s everything you need to know
Article Text:
Microsoft Copilot gets a new Home experience

Code lets users build apps and workflows

Autopilot can continue working on tasks

More business data and plugins

Microsoft updates Copilot AI spending controls

Microsoft has introduced a new version of Copilot. The latest version brings AI agents, Office tools and a new Code feature into a single experience. The tech giant is positioning the updated Copilot as a place where users can ask questions, delegate longer tasks, create documents and build small software solutions.The update adds three key capabilities: Home, Code and Autopilot. Home brings Chat and Cowork together, Office in Copilot adds Word, Excel and PowerPoint capabilities, while Code lets users create apps, dashboards and workflows using natural-language instructions. Meanwhile, Autopilot is designed to continue working on assigned tasks without requiring a new prompt each time.Microsoft has confirmed that Home will become Copilot's starting point, combining Chat and Cowork in one interface. Chat is designed for questions, lookups, and drafting, while Cowork handles multi-step tasks and produces a completed result.Microsoft said Copilot will eventually be able to determine whether a request should be handled by Chat, Cowork or Code, removing the need for users to select a mode themselves.The company is also bringing Office capabilities directly into Copilot. Users will be able to create or update Word documents, Excel workbooks and PowerPoint presentations from the Copilot interface.Files remain editable and can stay synchronised with the corresponding Microsoft 365 applications.The new Code feature aims to let non-developers create small, purpose-built software solutions. Users can describe an app, tracker, dashboard, automation or workflow in natural language, after which Copilot builds it.Microsoft said Code uses the same underlying technology as GitHub Copilot and operates in a sandboxed environment. Solutions can include desktop widgets, interactive dashboards and cloud-hosted internal applications.Code is scheduled to enter Microsoft's Frontier programme at the end of the month, with broader availability planned in the following weeks. A preview will also be available to Microsoft 365 Premium and Pro subscribers later this year.Microsoft is also introducing Copilot Managed Runtime, a hosting environment that lets applications created through Code, Cowork, and Copilot Studio run within an organisation's Microsoft 365 environment.Autopilot, previously known as Scout, is Microsoft's persistent agent designed to continue working after a user assigns it a goal. Users can give Autopilot a name, role and objective, after which it can monitor channels, follow up on conversations and handle recurring work. The agent operates in the cloud and has its own identity, memory, computer and workspace within the organisation's tenant.Microsoft said Autopilot is designed to work across Teams, Outlook, chats, channels and documents, while remaining subject to permissions, auditing and organisational controls. Autopilot will expand to private preview at the end of September.Microsoft is expanding Copilot's access to business context through Microsoft IQ. Fabric IQ brings data from Power BI semantic models into Copilot, while integration with Dynamics 365 and Power Platform is planned for public preview.A new plugin registry will also bring Microsoft, partner and custom-built plugins into one catalogue. Administrators can approve and manage plugins centrally.Microsoft is also adding FinOps capabilities for managing AI spending. The company is separating everyday Copilot use from longer-running agentic workloads.A user subscription license covers Copilot across applications such as Word, Excel, PowerPoint, Outlook and Teams. Usage-based billing applies to features including Cowork, Code and Autopilot.New administrative controls will let organisations manage spending policies, model availability, and credit requests. Users will also be able to see their credit usage, remaining balances and usage history within Copilot.Home and Code will begin rolling out through Microsoft's Frontier programme, while Autopilot is moving to private preview. Microsoft said it will continue rolling out additional Copilot features over the coming months.
Article Summary: Home brings Chat and Cowork together, Office in Copilot adds Word, Excel and PowerPoint capabilities. Code lets users create apps, dashboards and workflows using natural-language instructions. Autopilot is designed to continue working on assigned tasks without requiring a new prompt each time.

Article Title: OpenAI's AI agents hacked Australian government health website; alert email sent a month later to Public mailbox; upset Australian PM says: I spoke with Sam Altman to tell ...
Article Text:
Representative Image. In pic: Sam Altman

“Today, I spoke with the CEO of OpenAI,

Sam Altman

, to express Australia's extreme concern about this incident. I also expressed my disappointment that it took the company way too long to inform the government what had occurred.”

What happened during the OpenAI AI test

“didn't accept no for an answer”

OpenAI found the breach in August

“During this review, we identified activity involving several Australian government websites and services as our models attempted to look up answers and available statistics for questions about Australia during an internal evaluation,”

“In the course of that, our models took actions we did not intend,”

Australian government was notified through public mailbox

Australia launches investigation

ChatGPT maker OpenAI 's AI agents hacked Australian government health website. The incident happened in June, when an OpenAI model being evaluated for training was asked to research Australian government spending on medicines. According to Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese, the AI agent initially encountered restrictions on an Australian Medicare statistics portal but found a way around them and accessed public and non-public files.The Australian government says there is no evidence that any personal Medicare data was accessed. There has also been no breach of government systems. However, this issue has raised questions about how easily AI systems can bypass security measures. It has also raised questions about how long it takes for OpenAI to contact the authorities.According to a report by AFP, Albanese said,He added that the notification was also unacceptable because it was sent to a public mailbox rather than directly to the relevant government officials.The incident took place on June 18 while OpenAI was conducting internal evaluations of its AI models. Government Services Minister Katy Gallagher said the model had been asked to search for information about Australian government spending on medicines.The AI agent interacted with several government websites. On the Medicare statistics portal, it encountered restrictions but continued attempting to obtain information. Albanese described the model as havingand finding a way around the blocks.The accessed material included non-public aggregate health statistics and internal file names. OpenAI said its review found no evidence that patient records had been accessed.OpenAI did not identify the activity immediately. According to the Australian government, the company discovered the incident on August 11 while reviewing potentially misaligned model activity during training.OpenAI said it was conducting an extensive review of its models when it identified activity involving several Australian government websites and services. The company said its models were attempting to find answers and statistics about Australia during an internal evaluation.OpenAI said.the company added.Although OpenAI identified the incident in August, Australian authorities were not notified until September 10, almost a month later. The notification was sent to a public Services Australia mailbox that is used for reports from academics and researchers.Gallagher said the mailbox is checked once a day and can receive multiple notifications, including hoaxes. Services Australia reviewed the message before reporting the incident to Australia's cyber security agency on September 15.The timeline has become a major concern for the government. Albanese said the delay in reporting the incident was unacceptable, while OpenAI has said it is providing technical information to assist the investigation.Australia has launched a rapid review of the incident involving the prime minister's department, the Australian Signals Directorate and the country's AI Safety Institute. The review will examine what happened and whether existing rules adequately cover incidents involving autonomous AI systems.Deputy Prime Minister Richard Marles compared the incident to an AI system “scaling the fence” after being denied access. He said the breach was serious but that no personal information had been accessed.The incident comes as concerns grow over AI models interacting with real-world computer systems. OpenAI and Anthropic have both reported instances in which models gained unauthorised access during testing, while Google has also disclosed security-related activity involving its AI systems.OpenAI CEO Sam Altman was in New York for discussions on AI risks at the United Nations when the Australian government made the incident public. Albanese said he had spoken directly with Altman about Australia's concerns and the delay in notification.
Article Summary: ChatGPT maker OpenAI's AI agents hacked Australian government health website. The incident happened in June, when an OpenAI model was asked to research Australian government spending on medicines. The AI agent initially encountered restrictions on an Australian Medicare statistics portal but found a way around them.

Article Title: Peter Thiel to all billionaires and others blaming China for anti-AI backlash in America: Stop doing this, you cannot ...
Article Text:
Peter Thiel

Peter Thiel says US is largely responsible for AI backlash

AI debate increasingly linked to US-China rivalry

Peter Thiel has pushed back against claims that China is behind growing anti-AI sentiment in the US, saying Americans should look at their own actions instead. In an interview with Axel Springer CEO Mathias Döpfner on the “MD Meets” podcast recently, the PayPal co-founder said he is “inclined to believe” China could be fueling some anti-AI content, but does not see it as the main reason for the change in public sentiment. “This is mainly what we’re doing to ourselves,” Thiel said. “It’s often somewhat too easy to simply blame it on China.”Peter Thiel's comments come as some US technology executives have blamed China, America's main AI rival, for growing criticism of the technology. Thiel, who has himself been a strong critic of China, said the country should be taken seriously but argued against blaming it for every development around AI.Asked whether China was promoting anti-AI material on American social media, Thiel said he had not studied the issue closely. He said he was inclined to believe it was happening, but added that it was not the main factor behind the backlash.Thiel also criticised Pope Leo XIV's May 2026 AI encyclical, describing it as anti-AI. He argued that the Chinese Communist Party would not listen to the Pope, while people in the US might.“I'm not saying he was an agent of the communists,” Thiel said, “but he was at least acting as a useful idiot for the CCP.”Thiel later said he may have put the point too strongly, but repeated his argument that the Pope's message could have an effect in the US while China would not follow it.Thiel’s comments come as AI development has become closely tied to competition between the US and China. The US has accused Chinese AI companies of copying American AI technology, while China has rejected those claims.At the same time, concerns about AI's impact on jobs, safety, security and society have grown in the US. Thiel's argument is that those concerns should not automatically be attributed to Chinese influence. In the “MD Meets” interview, he said the US should instead examine how its own decisions and discussions are shaping public attitudes toward AI.
Article Summary: Peter Thiel says US is largely responsible for AI backlash. PayPal co-founder says he is 'inclined to believe' China could be fueling some anti-AI content. Thiel also criticised Pope Leo XIV's May 2026 AI encyclical as 'anti-AI'
